title: Τηλέμαχος ἐν σταθμῷ
titleEn: Telemachus at the Swineherd’s Hut — Odyssey 16.1–111
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Morning at the swineherd’s steading. Odysseus, still disguised as a beggar, and Eumaeus are making breakfast when the dogs fawn on a newcomer instead of barking: it is Telemachus, home from Pylos. Eumaeus drops what he is holding, weeps, and kisses him as a father welcomes a son returned after ten years, then asks him in and takes his spear. Odysseus rises to give his son his seat; Telemachus makes him stay, and Eumaeus spreads green twigs and a fleece for the young man. After the meal Telemachus asks where the stranger comes from, and Eumaeus tells the Cretan story the stranger gave and puts him in Telemachus’ hands as a suppliant. Telemachus answers that he is too young to defend a guest against the suitors, and that his mother is undecided whether to stay or marry; he promises the stranger clothes, a sword and sandals, but will not let him go to the suitors’ hall. Odysseus replies with questions about why Telemachus puts up with them, and says he would rather die in his own halls than watch their outrages.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ αὖτ’ ἐν κλισίῃ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ δῖος ὑφορβὸς
ἐντύνοντο ἄριστον ἅμ’ ἠοῖ, κηαμένω πῦρ,
ἔκπεμψάν τε νομῆας ἅμ’ ἀγρομένοισι σύεσσι·
sentences.tr:
tō d’ aut’ en klisiēi Odyseus kai dios hyphorbos
entynonto ariston ham’ ēoi, kēamenō pyr,
ekpempsan te nomēas ham’ agromenoisi syessi·
sentences.i: Meanwhile, in the hut, Odysseus and the heavenly swineherd were preparing breakfast at dawn, having kindled a fire, and they sent the herdsmen out with the gathered swine;
sentences.n: The scene is the swineherd’s hut at dawn. τώ is the dual of the article-form used as a pronoun, ‘the two’. ἐντύνοντο is the imperfect middle of ἐντύνω ‘make ready’; ἄριστον is the early meal. κηαμένω is a dual aorist middle participle of καίω in its epic form, ‘having kindled’. ἠοῖ is the dative of ἠώς. νομῆας is the Ionic accusative plural of νομεύς ‘herdsman’; σύεσσι is the dative plural of σῦς ‘swine’, and ἀγρομένοισι the dative plural of the aorist middle participle of ἀγείρω, ‘gathered together’. The first line is found elsewhere in the poem, where δορπείτην ‘were having supper’ follows it.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχον δὲ περίσσαινον κύνες ὑλακόμωροι,
οὐδ’ ὕλαον προσιόντα.
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachon de perissainon kynes hylakomōroi,
oud’ hylaon prosionta.
sentences.l:
And around Telemachus fawned the barking dogs,
nor did they bark at him as he approached.
sentences.i: The barking dogs fawned round Telemachus and did not bark at him as he approached.
sentences.n: Telemachus’ arrival is told first through the dogs. περίσσαινον is the imperfect of περισαίνω ‘fawn around’, as dogs do to someone they know. κύνες ὑλακόμωροι is a standing phrase: ὑλακο- is ‘barking’, and the second element -μωρος is of unknown meaning, so only the barking is translated. ὕλαον is the imperfect of ὑλάω ‘bark’. προσιόντα is the accusative participle of πρόσειμι ‘approach’, agreeing with Τηλέμαχον, the unexpressed object of ὕλαον. The unit ends in the middle of line 5, at the full stop.

sentences.t:
νόησε δὲ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
σαίνοντάς τε κύνας, περί τε κτύπος ἦλθε ποδοῖϊν.
sentences.tr:
noēse de dios Odysseus
sainontas te kynas, peri te ktypos ēlthe podoiïn.
sentences.l:
and noticed heavenly Odysseus
the dogs fawning, and about came the thud of feet.
sentences.i: Heavenly Odysseus noticed the dogs fawning, and there came the sound of feet.
sentences.n: νόησε is the aorist of νοέω ‘notice’ without augment. σαίνοντάς … κύνας is an accusative participle phrase, ‘the dogs fawning’; the first τε is answered by the second, so Odysseus notices the dogs and the sound of feet comes. κτύπος is a beating sound, a thud. ποδοῖϊν is a dual form (Attic ποδοῖν), ‘of the two feet’. The exact force of περί is not certain: it seems to be an adverb ‘round about’, and l keeps ‘about’. The unit begins in the middle of line 5.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἄρ’ Εὔμαιον ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: aipsa d’ ar’ Eumaion epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: And at once then, to Eumaeus, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: At once he spoke winged words to Eumaeus:
sentences.n: The subject, Odysseus, is not named; the speech follows in the next unit. αἶψα is ‘at once’; ἄρα ‘then’ marks the next step. Εὔμαιον is the accusative of the person spoken to, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα, ‘winged words’, is the formula that introduces a speech; the English keeps ‘winged’ every time. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’.

sentences.t:
Εὔμαι’, ἦ μάλα τίς τοι ἐλεύσεται ἐνθάδ’ ἑταῖρος
ἢ καὶ γνώριμος ἄλλος, ἐπεὶ κύνες οὐχ ὑλάουσιν,
ἀλλὰ περισσαίνουσι·
sentences.tr:
Eumai’, ē mala tis toi eleusetai enthad’ hetairos
ē kai gnōrimos allos, epei kynes ouch hylaousin,
alla perissainousi·
sentences.i: “Eumaeus, surely some companion of yours is coming here, or some other acquaintance, since the dogs are not barking but fawning all round;
sentences.n: Odysseus reasons from the dogs’ behaviour. Εὔμαι’ is the vocative Εὔμαιε with its final vowel elided. ἦ μάλα ‘truly’ opens with emphasis; τοι is the enclitic dative σοι, ‘of yours’. ἐλεύσεται is a future, a confident guess. γνώριμος ‘acquaintance’ is a person known to you; ἢ καί ‘or even’. ὑλάουσιν is uncontracted (Attic ὑλῶσιν). περισσαίνουσι is the verb of line 4 in the present, and the unit ends at the high stop.

sentences.t: ποδῶν δ’ ὑπὸ δοῦπον ἀκούω.
sentences.tr: podōn d’ hypo doupon akouō.
sentences.l: and of feet, beneath, the thud I hear.”
sentences.i: and I hear the thud of footsteps.”
sentences.n: Odysseus hears footsteps before he sees anyone. ποδῶν is the genitive plural of πούς, ‘of feet’, and δοῦπος is a heavy dull sound, a thud. The force of ὑπό is not certain: it may go with ἀκούω as a tmesis (‘catch the sound’), or with δοῦπον (the sound ‘beneath’ the walkers). l keeps ‘beneath’ and i leaves it out. The unit begins in the middle of line 10 and closes Odysseus’ speech.

sentences.t:
οὔ πω πᾶν εἴρητο ἔπος, ὅτε οἱ φίλος υἱὸς
ἔστη ἐνὶ προθύροισι.
sentences.tr:
ou pō pan eirēto epos, hote hoi philos huios
estē eni prothyroisi.
sentences.l:
Not yet the whole word had been spoken, when his dear son
stood in the forecourt.
sentences.i: He had not yet finished speaking when his dear son stood in the forecourt.
sentences.n: Murray begins a new paragraph. οὔ πω is ‘not yet’. εἴρητο is the pluperfect passive of εἴρω ‘say’ (the verb whose future is ἐρῶ), so ‘had been spoken’. οἱ is the enclitic dative ‘his’, Odysseus’ own; the son is Telemachus, named in line 4 and not again until line 20. ἔστη is the aorist ‘stood’; προθύροισι is the dative plural of πρόθυρον ‘forecourt’ in -οισι. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of line 12.

sentences.t:
ταφὼν δ’ ἀνόρουσε συβώτης,
ἐκ δ’ ἄρα οἱ χειρῶν πέσον ἄγγεα, τοῖς ἐπονεῖτο,
κιρνὰς αἴθοπα οἶνον.
sentences.tr:
taphōn d’ anorouse sybōtēs,
ek d’ ara hoi cheirōn peson angea, tois eponeito,
kirnas aithopa oinon.
sentences.l:
And astounded leapt up the swineherd,
and out of his hands fell the vessels, with which he was busy,
mixing the fire-faced wine.
sentences.i: The swineherd leapt up in astonishment, and the vessels he was busy with, as he mixed the wine that has the look of fire, fell from his hands.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 12. ταφών is the aorist participle of an old verb whose other main form is the perfect τέθηπα, ‘astounded’. ἀνόρουσε is an aorist of ἀνορούω ‘leap up’. ἐκ … πέσον is tmesis (ἐκπίπτω ‘fall out’), πέσον without augment; οἱ is ‘his’. ἄγγεα are ‘vessels’, and τοῖς is a relative, ‘with which’. κιρνάς is the participle of κίρνημι ‘mix’ wine with water. αἴθοπα οἶνον is ‘fire-faced wine’, built like οἶνοψ πόντος, with the look of fire.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἀντίος ἦλθεν ἄνακτος,
κύσσε δέ μιν κεφαλήν τε καὶ ἄμφω φάεα καλὰ
χεῖράς τ’ ἀμφοτέρας·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ antios ēlthen anaktos,
kysse de min kephalēn te kai amphō phaea kala
cheiras t’ amphoteras·
sentences.i: He went to meet his lord and kissed him on the head, and on both his beautiful eyes, and on both his hands;
sentences.n: ὁ δέ marks the change of subject: the swineherd now moves, and Telemachus is his ἄναξ ‘lord’. ἀντίος ‘face to face, to meet’ takes the genitive ἄνακτος. κύσσε is the aorist of κυνέω ‘kiss’ without augment. κεφαλήν, φάεα and χεῖρας are accusatives naming the parts kissed, all beside μιν ‘him’. φάεα ‘lights’ is the plural of φάος, used for the eyes. The unit begins in the middle of line 14.

sentences.t: θαλερὸν δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε δάκρυ.
sentences.tr: thaleron de hoi ekpese dakry.
sentences.l: and for him an abundant tear fell out.
sentences.i: and abundant tears fell from him.
sentences.n: θαλερόν ‘abundant’ qualifies the tear; the singular δάκρυ is collective, so i says ‘tears’. οἱ is the dative ‘from him’ (the person affected). ἔκπεσε is the aorist of ἐκπίπτω ‘fall out’, with no augment. The unit begins in the middle of line 16; the cause of the tears is given in the simile that follows.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ πατὴρ ὃν παῖδα φίλα φρονέων ἀγαπάζῃ
ἐλθόντ’ ἐξ ἀπίης γαίης δεκάτῳ ἐνιαυτῷ,
μοῦνον τηλύγετον, τῷ ἔπ’ ἄλγεα πολλὰ μογήσῃ,
sentences.tr:
hōs de patēr hon paida phila phroneōn agapazēi
elthont’ ex apiēs gaiēs dekatōi eniautōi,
mounon tēlygeton, tōi ep’ algea polla mogēsēi,
sentences.l:
And as a father his own son, kindly thinking, welcomes warmly,
come from a far-off land in the tenth year,
only, late-born, for whom many pains he has toiled through,
sentences.i: As a father with kindly thoughts welcomes warmly his own son, come from a far-off land in the tenth year, his only, late-born child, for whom he has toiled through many pains,
sentences.n: A simile begins: ὡς δέ ‘and as’. ὅν is the possessive ‘his own’, not a relative. φίλα φρονέων ‘thinking kindly’. ἀγαπάζῃ is a subjunctive without ἄν, as in a general comparison. ἀπίης γαίης is ‘a far-off land’; δεκάτῳ ἐνιαυτῷ is a dative of time. τηλύγετος is a word of uncertain meaning: ‘late-born’ is the usual gloss, and the rendering used at 4.11, while ‘far-grown’ and ‘tenderly reared’ have also been proposed. ἔπ’ is ἐπί placed after τῷ: ‘for whom’. μογήσῃ is a subjunctive of μογέω ‘toil’. The sentence is cut at this comma because it would otherwise run to five lines.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότε Τηλέμαχον θεοειδέα δῖος ὑφορβὸς
πάντα κύσεν περιφύς, ὡς ἐκ θανάτοιο φυγόντα·
sentences.tr:
hōs tote Tēlemachon theoeidea dios hyphorbos
panta kysen periphys, hōs ek thanatoio phygonta·
sentences.l:
so then Telemachus godlike-in-form the heavenly swineherd
kissed all over, having clung round him, as one escaped from death;
sentences.i: so the heavenly swineherd clung round Telemachus, godlike in form, and kissed him all over, as if he had escaped from death;
sentences.n: ὣς τότε ‘so then’ answers the ὡς of line 17 and closes the comparison. θεοειδέα ‘godlike in form’ is Telemachus’ epithet, kept each time. δῖος ὑφορβός is ‘the heavenly swineherd’. πάντα is adverbial, ‘all over’. κύσεν is the aorist of κυνέω; περιφύς, the aorist participle of περιφύομαι ‘grow round’, means clinging to him. ὡς ἐκ θανάτοιο φυγόντα ‘as one who had escaped from death’: ὡς with a participle gives the supposed reason, and θανάτοιο is a genitive in -οιο.

sentences.t: καί ῥ’ ὀλοφυρόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: kai rh’ olophyromenos epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and so, lamenting, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: And, lamenting, he spoke winged words:
sentences.n: καὶ ῥ’ is καὶ ῥα ‘and so’. ὀλοφυρόμενος ‘lamenting’ is a middle participle, here of joyful grief, since Eumaeus weeps for gladness. The line is the same formula as line 7, with no person named: ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’. The speaker is Eumaeus and his words are addressed to Telemachus.

sentences.t: ἦλθες, Τηλέμαχε, γλυκερὸν φάος.
sentences.tr: ēlthes, Tēlemache, glykeron phaos.
sentences.l: “You have come, Telemachus, sweet light.
sentences.i: “You have come, Telemachus, my sweet light.
sentences.n: Murray begins a new paragraph. ἦλθες is the aorist ‘you have come’. γλυκερὸν φάος ‘sweet light’ stands in apposition to the person addressed: Telemachus is Eumaeus’ light, a term of love, as the light of the sun is dear to the living. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of line 23.

sentences.t:
οὔ σ’ ἔτ’ ἐγώ γε
ὄψεσθαι ἐφάμην, ἐπεὶ ᾤχεο νηῒ Πύλονδε.
sentences.tr:
ou s’ et’ egō ge
opsesthai ephamēn, epei ōicheo nēï Pylonde.
sentences.l:
Not you any more I, at least,
thought to see, since you were gone by ship to Pylos.
sentences.i: I did not think I should see you again, since you had gone off by ship to Pylos.
sentences.n: ἐφάμην is the imperfect middle of φημί; with a future infinitive it means ‘I thought I should…’, so ‘I did not expect to see you’. οὔ … ἔτι is ‘not any more’; ἐγώ γε is ‘I at least’. ὄψεσθαι is the future infinitive of ὁράω. ᾤχεο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘be gone, be away’. νηῒ is the dative of ναῦς ‘ship’. Πύλονδε has the suffix -δε ‘towards’: ‘to Pylos’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν εἴσελθε, φίλον τέκος, ὄφρα σε θυμῷ
τέρψομαι εἰσορόων νέον ἄλλοθεν ἔνδον ἐόντα.
sentences.tr:
all’ age nyn eiselthe, philon tekos, ophra se thymōi
terpsomai eisoroōn neon allothen endon eonta.
sentences.l:
But come now, go in, dear child, so that in my heart
I may take delight, gazing at you, newly from elsewhere being inside.
sentences.i: But come now, go in, dear child, so that I may take delight in my heart, gazing at you, newly come from elsewhere and now inside.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ‘but come now’ introduces the imperative εἴσελθε ‘go in’. φίλον τέκος is a fond address. ὄφρα takes τέρψομαι (a future or a short-vowel subjunctive) ‘so that I may delight’, with θυμῷ ‘in my heart’; εἰσορόων is the uncontracted participle of εἰσοράω (Attic εἰσορῶν), taking σε. νέον is an adverb ‘newly’; ἄλλοθεν is ‘from elsewhere’ with the suffix -θεν; ἔνδον ἐόντα ‘being inside’ pictures Telemachus once he has come in.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τι θάμ’ ἀγρὸν ἐπέρχεαι οὐδὲ νομῆας,
ἀλλ’ ἐπιδημεύεις·
sentences.tr:
ou men gar ti tham’ agron epercheai oude nomēas,
all’ epidēmeueis·
sentences.l:
For not at all often the farm do you go to, nor the herdsmen,
but you stay in the town;
sentences.i: For you do not often come out to the farm or to the herdsmen, but stay in the town;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι ‘for not at all’. θάμ’ is θαμά ‘often’. ἐπέρχεαι is the second singular with the uncontracted ending -εαι (Attic ἐπέρχῃ), and its objects are ἀγρόν ‘farm, field’ and νομῆας ‘herdsmen’. ἐπιδημεύεις is built on δῆμος and means to be at home among the people, in the town, here in contrast to the farm. The unit ends at the high stop in the middle of line 28.

sentences.t:
ὣς γάρ νύ τοι εὔαδε θυμῷ,
ἀνδρῶν μνηστήρων ἐσορᾶν ἀΐδηλον ὅμιλον.
sentences.tr:
hōs gar ny toi euade thymōi,
andrōn mnēstērōn esoran aïdēlon homilon.
sentences.l:
for so, indeed, it has pleased you in your heart
to look upon the destroying throng of suitor men.”
sentences.i: for so it has pleased your heart, to look upon the destructive crowd of suitors.”
sentences.n: ὣς γάρ νύ τοι ‘for so, you see, to you’: νυ is a particle, τοι is σοι. εὔαδε is an aorist of ἁνδάνω ‘please’, and ἐσορᾶν the infinitive of εἰσοράω ‘look at’ in its epic spelling with ἐσ-. ἀΐδηλον is of uncertain meaning (‘destroying’ is the traditional sense; ‘making unseen’ is the guessed origin), and ὅμιλος is a throng. The sentence reads as a mild reproach. The unit begins in the middle of line 28 and closes Eumaeus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A formula that returns each time Telemachus replies: τὸν δ’ αὖ ‘to him in turn’, ἀντίον ‘face to face’, ηὔδα the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’. πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is his standing epithet and is translated every time. The same line is found elsewhere in the poem with the same English.

sentences.t: ἔσσεται οὕτως, ἄττα·
sentences.tr: essetai houtōs, atta·
sentences.l: “It shall be so, father;
sentences.i: “So it shall be, father;
sentences.n: Telemachus accepts Eumaeus’ invitation to come in. ἔσσεται is the future of εἰμί with a doubled σ (Attic ἔσται). ἄττα is a respectful, affectionate address from a younger man to an older one; ‘father’ is the conventional English and claims no kinship. The unit is the first half of line 31, closed by the high stop.

sentences.t:
σέθεν δ’ ἕνεκ’ ἐνθάδ’ ἱκάνω,
ὄφρα σέ τ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἴδω καὶ μῦθον ἀκούσω,
sentences.tr:
sethen d’ henek’ enthad’ hikanō,
ophra se t’ ophthalmoisin idō kai mython akousō,
sentences.l:
and for your sake I come here,
so that both you with my eyes I may see, and a word may hear,
sentences.i: and it is for your sake that I have come here, to see you with my own eyes and to hear a word from you,
sentences.n: σέθεν is the genitive σοῦ, and σέθεν ἕνεκ’ means ‘for your sake’. ἱκάνω is a present, ‘I come’, here with the sense ‘I have come’. ὄφρα takes the subjunctives ἴδω and ἀκούσω ‘so that I may see … hear’. ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is a dative in -οισι(ν). σέ τε … καὶ μῦθον joins the two things sought, the sight of Eumaeus and his word. The sentence is cut at this comma because the indirect question that follows takes three more lines.

sentences.t:
ἤ μοι ἔτ’ ἐν μεγάροις μήτηρ μένει, ἦέ τις ἤδη
ἀνδρῶν ἄλλος ἔγημεν, Ὀδυσσῆος δέ που εὐνὴ
χήτει ἐνευναίων κάκ’ ἀράχνια κεῖται ἔχουσα.
sentences.tr:
ē moi et’ en megarois mētēr menei, ēe tis ēdē
andrōn allos egēmen, Odyssēos de pou eunē
chētei eneunaiōn kak’ arachnia keitai echousa.
sentences.l:
whether for me still in the halls my mother remains, or whether already
another of the men has married, and Odysseus’ bed, I suppose,
for lack of bed-sharers lies holding evil cobwebs.”
sentences.i: whether my mother still stays in the halls, or whether some other man has married her by now, and the bed of Odysseus, I suppose, lies with foul cobwebs on it for want of anyone to sleep in it.”
sentences.n: The question has two alternatives. ἤ … ἦε is ‘whether … or whether’; the ἤ here is not the emphatic ἦ ‘truly’. ἔγημεν is the aorist of γαμέω ‘marry’, said of a man. που ‘I suppose’. χήτει ‘for lack of’ is a dative with the genitive ἐνευναίων ‘those who lie in it’, bed-sharers. κάκ’ is κακά, ‘evil, foul’, with the neuter plural ἀράχνια ‘cobwebs’. Ὀδυσσῆος has a doubled σ, as at line 48. The unit begins at line 33 and closes Telemachus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε συβώτης, ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe sybōtēs, orchamos andrōn·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the swineherd, chief of men:
sentences.i: Then the swineherd, chief of men, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A reply-formula, kept the same each time: τὸν δ’ αὖτε ‘him then in turn’ and προσέειπε ‘addressed’. ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν ‘chief of men’ is Eumaeus’ standing title, and συβώτης is ‘swineherd’. Murray begins a new paragraph. The same line is found elsewhere in the poem with the same English.

sentences.t:
καὶ λίην κείνη γε μένει τετληότι θυμῷ
σοῖσιν ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν·
sentences.tr:
kai liēn keinē ge menei tetlēoti thymōi
soisin eni megaroisin·
sentences.l:
‘Yes, very much, she stays, with enduring heart,
in your halls;
sentences.i: ‘Yes, she stays there, truly, with an enduring heart, in your halls;
sentences.n: Eumaeus answers about Penelope. καὶ λίην ‘yes, very much’. κείνη is the Ionic form of ἐκείνη ‘she’. τετληότι θυμῷ ‘with an enduring heart’: τετληότι is the perfect participle of τλάω ‘endure’, in the dative to agree with θυμῷ. σοῖσιν is the dative plural of σός ‘your’, and ἐνί is ἐν. The unit closes at the high stop in the middle of line 38. The same words are found elsewhere in the poem with the same English, including its single quotation mark (there they stand inside another speech); this speech closes with the matching mark at line 39.

sentences.t:
ὀϊζυραὶ δέ οἱ αἰεὶ
φθίνουσιν νύκτες τε καὶ ἤματα δάκρυ χεούσῃ.
sentences.tr:
oïzyrai de hoi aiei
phthinousin nyktes te kai ēmata dakry cheousēi.
sentences.l:
and sorrowful for her always
waste away the nights and the days, a tear shedding.’
sentences.i: and for her the nights and days are always sorrowful, and wear away as she sheds tears.’
sentences.n: οἱ is the dative ‘for her’ and the participle χεούσῃ agrees with it, ‘for her, shedding a tear’; the singular δάκρυ stands for tears. ὀϊζυραί ‘sorrowful’ is from ὀϊζύς ‘distress’; αἰεί is ‘always’. φθίνουσιν ‘waste away’ is said of the nights and days, which wear out as she weeps. ἤματα is the epic plural of ἦμαρ ‘day’. The unit begins in the middle of line 38 and closes Eumaeus’ speech. The same lines are found elsewhere in the poem with the same English.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας οἱ ἐδέξατο χάλκεον ἔγχος·
sentences.tr: hōs ara phōnēsas hoi edexato chalkeon enchos·
sentences.l: So then having spoken, from him he received the bronze spear;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and took the bronze spear from him;
sentences.n: The subject is Eumaeus, who takes Telemachus’ spear as he comes in; οἱ is ‘from him’, Telemachus. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is the formula for ‘so he spoke, and’. ἐδέξατο is the aorist of δέχομαι ‘receive’. ἔγχος is a spear, and χάλκεον ‘of bronze’ has the uncontracted ending (Attic χαλκοῦν). The same first half of the line is found elsewhere in the poem, followed by a different second line.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ εἴσω ἴεν καὶ ὑπέρβη λάϊνον οὐδόν.
sentences.tr: autar ho g’ eisō ien kai hyperbē laïnon oudon.
sentences.l: but he inside went, and stepped over the stone threshold.
sentences.i: and he went inside and stepped over the stone threshold.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but, and then’. ὅ γε is ‘he’, Telemachus, as the pronoun use of the article often is. εἴσω is ‘inside’. ἴεν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’ (Attic ᾔει), and ὑπέρβη an aorist of ὑπερβαίνω ‘step over’ with no augment. λάϊνον ‘of stone’ (λάας) is written with a diaeresis. The stone threshold is the sill of the doorway into the hut’s interior.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἕδρης ἐπιόντι πατὴρ ὑπόειξεν Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: tōi d’ hedrēs epionti patēr hypoeixen Odysseus·
sentences.l: and to him coming up, from his seat, his father Odysseus gave way;
sentences.i: and as he came up, his father Odysseus gave up his seat to him;
sentences.n: Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, is named ‘father’ by the poet, though Telemachus does not know him. τῷ ἐπιόντι is a dative participle of ἔπειμι, ‘to him as he approached’. ἕδρης is a genitive of separation, ‘from his seat’, and ὑπόειξεν the aorist of ὑπείκω ‘yield, give way’. The unit ends at the high stop.

sentences.t: Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐρήτυε φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: Tēlemachos d’ heterōthen erētye phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: and Telemachus from the other side held him back and spoke:
sentences.i: Telemachus held him back from the other side, and spoke:
sentences.n: Telemachus stops the old stranger from giving up his place. ἑτέρωθεν is ‘from the other side’ (suffix -θεν). ἐρήτυε is an imperfect of ἐρητύω ‘hold back, restrain’, a trying imperfect: he tries to stop him. φώνησέν τε is φώνησε ‘spoke’ with a movable ν and the enclitic τε, which gives the word a second accent on its last syllable.

sentences.t: ἧσ’, ὦ ξεῖν’·
sentences.tr: hēs’, ō xein’·
sentences.l: “Sit, O stranger;
sentences.i: “Stay seated, stranger;
sentences.n: Murray begins a new paragraph. ἧσ’ is ἧσο, the imperative of ἧμαι ‘sit’, ‘stay seated’. ὦ ξεῖν’ is ὦ ξεῖνε with the final vowel elided: ‘stranger’, the courteous address to a guest. The unit is the first half of line 44, closed by the high stop.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ ἄλλοθι δήομεν ἕδρην
σταθμῷ ἐν ἡμετέρῳ·
sentences.tr:
hēmeis de kai allothi dēomen hedrēn
stathmōi en hēmeterōi·
sentences.l:
and we elsewhere also shall find a seat
in our steading;
sentences.i: we shall find a seat elsewhere too, in our steading;
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς δέ ‘but we’. ἄλλοθι is ‘elsewhere’ (suffix -θι ‘where’). δήομεν is a form of the old verb δήω ‘find’, with future sense. ἕδρην is the accusative of ἕδρη ‘seat’. σταθμῷ ἐν ἡμετέρῳ ‘in our steading’: σταθμός is the farm-buildings, and Telemachus speaks of it as ‘ours’. The unit ends at the high stop in the middle of line 45.

sentences.t: πάρα δ’ ἀνὴρ ὃς καταθήσει.
sentences.tr: para d’ anēr hos katathēsei.
sentences.l: and at hand is a man who will lay one down.”
sentences.i: and there is a man at hand who will set one down.”
sentences.n: πάρα is πάρεστι ‘is at hand’, with the accent thrown back. ἀνήρ is Eumaeus himself, the man at hand. καταθήσει is the future of κατατίθημι ‘set down’, in a relative clause of purpose; the object ἕδρην is understood from the line before. The unit closes Telemachus’ speech, and Murray’s paragraph.

sentences.t: ὣς φάθ’, ὁ δ’ αὖτις ἰὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο·
sentences.tr: hōs phath’, ho d’ autis iōn kat’ ar’ hezeto·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and he, going back again, sat down;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Odysseus went back and sat down;
sentences.n: Murray begins a new paragraph. ὣς φάθ’ is ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’, the τ made a θ before the rough breathing of ὁ. ὁ δέ marks the change of subject to Odysseus. ἰών is a participle of εἶμι ‘go’ and αὖτις is ‘again, back’. κατ’ … ἕζετο is tmesis for κατέζετο ‘sat down’. The unit ends at the high stop in the middle of line 46.

sentences.t:
τῷ δὲ συβώτης.
χεῦεν ὕπο χλωρὰς ῥῶπας καὶ κῶας ὕπερθεν·
sentences.tr:
tōi de sybōtēs.
cheuen hypo chlōras rhōpas kai kōas hyperthen·
sentences.l:
and for him the swineherd
poured underneath green twigs, and a fleece on top;
sentences.i: and the swineherd heaped green twigs under him, with a fleece on top;
sentences.n: Murray prints a full stop after συβώτης, though τῷ δὲ συβώτης … χεῦεν is one sentence; the two lines are joined in one unit and l and i run on without a stop. χεῦεν is an aorist of χέω ‘pour, heap’. ὕπο is an adverb ‘underneath’. ῥῶπες are twigs, brushwood, and χλωρός ‘green’ here means fresh. κῶας is a fleece. Eumaeus makes Odysseus a seat of twigs and sheepskin. The unit begins in the middle of line 46.

sentences.t: ἔνθα καθέζετ’ ἔπειτα Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός.
sentences.tr: entha kathezet’ epeita Odyssēos philos huios.
sentences.l: There then sat down Odysseus’ dear son.
sentences.i: There the dear son of Odysseus sat down.
sentences.n: ἔνθα ‘there’ points to the seat just made. καθέζετ’ is the imperfect of καθέζομαι ‘sit down’, elided, used here for the act. Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός ‘the dear son of Odysseus’ is the standing phrase for Telemachus, whose name is left out. Ὀδυσσῆος has the doubled σ, a metrical variant of Ὀδυσῆος in line 100.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ αὖ κρειῶν πίνακας παρέθηκε συβώτης
ὀπταλέων, ἅ ῥα τῇ προτέρῃ ὑπέλειπον ἔδοντες,
σῖτον δ’ ἐσσυμένως παρενήνεεν ἐν κανέοισιν,
ἐν δ’ ἄρα κισσυβίῳ κίρνη μελιηδέα οἶνον·
sentences.tr:
toisin d’ au kreiōn pinakas parethēke sybōtēs
optaleōn, ha rha tēi proterēi hypeleipon edontes,
siton d’ essymenōs parenēneen en kaneoisin,
en d’ ara kissybiōi kirnē meliēdea oinon·
sentences.l:
And for them in turn platters of meats set beside the swineherd,
roast ones, which on the day before they had left over, eating,
and food hurriedly he heaped up beside in baskets,
and in an ivy-wood bowl he mixed honey-sweet wine;
sentences.i: The swineherd set before them platters of roast meats, left over from their eating the day before, and in haste heaped food beside them in baskets, and mixed honey-sweet wine in an ivy-wood bowl;
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is ‘for them’, Odysseus and Telemachus, now seated. κρειῶν is the genitive plural of κρέας ‘meat’, ὀπταλέων ‘roasted’. The relative ἅ takes up the meat: ὑπέλειπον ‘they were leaving over’, ἔδοντες ‘eating’, τῇ προτέρῃ (sc. ἡμέρᾳ) ‘on the day before’. σῖτον is ‘food’, κάνεα ‘baskets’ (dative κανέοισιν), ἐσσυμένως ‘hurriedly’. κισσύβιον ‘ivy-wood bowl’ is so named by the traditional explanation. κίρνη is an imperfect of κίρνημι ‘mix’. The bowl line is found elsewhere in the poem with the same English.

sentences.t: αὐτὸς δ’ ἀντίον ἷζεν Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο.
sentences.tr: autos d’ antion hizen Odyssēos theioio.
sentences.l: and himself he sat down opposite divine Odysseus.
sentences.i: and he himself sat down opposite divine Odysseus.
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘himself’ is the swineherd. ἀντίον ‘opposite’ takes the genitive Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο ‘divine Odysseus’; the genitives are in -οιο, Attic -ου. The narrator names the beggar Odysseus, though the others in the hut do not know it. ἷζεν is the imperfect of ἵζω ‘sit down’, and θεῖος is ‘divine’.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ep’ oneiath’ hetoima prokeimena cheiras iallon.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: A line of the meal, heard whenever food is set out. ἐπ’ … ἴαλλον is tmesis for ἐπιάλλω ‘send upon’, so ‘stretched out their hands to’. ὀνείαθ’ is ὀνείατα, ‘good things’, food. ἑτοῖμα ‘ready’ and προκείμενα ‘lying before them’ qualify it. ἴαλλον is the imperfect of ἰάλλω. The same line is found elsewhere in the poem with the same English.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
δὴ τότε Τηλέμαχος προσεφώνεε δῖον ὑφορβόν·
sentences.tr:
autar epei posios kai edētyos ex eron hento,
dē tote Tēlemachos prosephōnee dion hyphorbon·
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
then indeed Telemachus spoke to the heavenly swineherd:
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, Telemachus then spoke to the heavenly swineherd:
sentences.n: The first line is the formula for the end of a meal: πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος are genitives (‘of drink and of food’), and ἔρον ἕντο ‘put away desire’ is an aorist middle of ἵημι with tmesis (ἐξ … ἕντο). δὴ τότε ‘then indeed’ opens the main clause. προσεφώνεε is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’. ὑφορβός ‘swineherd’ is a second word for the same man as συβώτης.

sentences.t: ἄττα, πόθεν τοι ξεῖνος ὅδ’ ἵκετο;
sentences.tr: atta, pothen toi xeinos hod’ hiketo;
sentences.l: “Father, whence to you did this stranger come?
sentences.i: “Father, where has this stranger of yours come from?
sentences.n: Murray begins a new paragraph. ἄττα ‘father’ is the address of line 31 again. πόθεν ‘from where’ has the suffix -θεν. τοι is σοι, ‘of yours’. ὅδ’ is ὅδε ‘this’. ἵκετο is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘arrive’; the metre needs its ι long, and that lengthening is the augment, which the spelling cannot show. ξεῖνος here is a stranger of unknown origin, not yet a guest-friend. The unit ends at the Greek question mark.

sentences.t:
πῶς δέ ἑ ναῦται
ἤγαγον εἰς Ἰθάκην;
sentences.tr:
pōs de he nautai
ēgagon eis Ithakēn;
sentences.l:
And how him sailors
brought to Ithaca?
sentences.i: And how did sailors bring him to Ithaca?
sentences.n: πῶς δέ ‘and how’. ἑ is the accusative of the third-person pronoun, ‘him’, an enclitic. ναῦται ‘sailors’. ἤγαγον is the aorist of ἄγω ‘bring, lead’. Ithaca is an island, which is why the stranger’s way of getting there matters. The unit begins in the middle of line 57 and ends at the question mark.

sentences.t: τίνες ἔμμεναι εὐχετόωντο;
sentences.tr: tines emmenai euchetoōnto;
sentences.l: Who did they declare themselves to be?
sentences.i: Who did they declare themselves to be?
sentences.n: τίνες ‘who’ is the predicate of ἔμμεναι, the epic infinitive of εἰμί (Attic εἶναι). εὐχετόωντο is the imperfect of εὐχετάομαι, a form of εὔχομαι ‘declare, claim’, with the uncontracted ending -όωντο. Telemachus asks what the sailors said about themselves, that is, whose people they claimed to be. The unit begins in the middle of line 58.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τί ἑ πεζὸν ὀΐομαι ἐνθάδ’ ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.tr: ou men gar ti he pezon oïomai enthad’ hikesthai.
sentences.l: For not at all him on foot do I suppose to have come here.”
sentences.i: For I do not at all suppose that he came here on foot.”
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι ‘for not at all’, as at line 27. ἑ is ‘him’ again, the subject of the infinitive. πεζόν ‘on foot’ is a predicate accusative. ὀΐομαι is ‘I suppose’, and ἱκέσθαι the aorist infinitive of ἱκνέομαι ‘to have come’. Ithaca is an island, so the stranger must have arrived by sea. The unit closes Telemachus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephēs, Eumaie sybōta·
sentences.l: Him, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: The poet turns to Eumaeus as ‘you’. προσέφης is the second person of the imperfect προσέφην ‘address’ (πρόσφημι), and ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is a middle participle. Εὔμαιε συβῶτα is a vocative, the second word in -α (nominative συβώτης). Murray begins a new paragraph. The same line is found elsewhere in the poem with the same English.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, τέκνον, ἀληθέα πάντ’ ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.tr: toigar egō toi, teknon, alēthea pant’ agoreusō.
sentences.l: “Well then, I will tell you, child, all the truth.
sentences.i: “Well then, my child, I will tell you the whole truth.
sentences.n: Eumaeus answers Telemachus’ questions. τοιγάρ ‘well then’. ἐγώ τοι ‘I to you’, with τοι for σοι. τέκνον is ‘child’. ἀληθέα is uncontracted (Attic ἀληθῆ), and ἀγορεύσω a future ‘I will tell’. The line is found elsewhere in the poem with the same English.

sentences.t:
ἐκ μὲν Κρητάων γένος εὔχεται εὐρειάων,
φησὶ δὲ πολλὰ βροτῶν ἐπὶ ἄστεα δινηθῆναι
πλαζόμενος·
sentences.tr:
ek men Krētaōn genos euchetai eureiaōn,
phēsi de polla brotōn epi astea dinēthēnai
plazomenos·
sentences.i: He declares his birth to be from broad Crete, and says he has been whirled about to many cities of mortals, roaming;
sentences.n: Eumaeus relates the stranger’s tale. Κρητάων εὐρειάων is a genitive plural, Crete named in a plural form that is not explained; the sense is ‘broad Crete’. γένος εὔχεται ‘declares his birth’ (εὔχομαι ‘declare’). φησί introduces the infinitive δινηθῆναι, the aorist passive of δινέω ‘whirl’: ‘to have been whirled about’. πλαζόμενος ‘roaming’ is the present passive participle of πλάζω. The unit ends at the high stop in the middle of line 64.

sentences.t: ὣς γάρ οἱ ἐπέκλωσεν τά γε δαίμων.
sentences.tr: hōs gar hoi epeklōsen ta ge daimōn.
sentences.l: for so for him spun these things some power.
sentences.i: for so some power spun these things for him.
sentences.n: ὣς γάρ ‘for thus’ gives the reason for the wandering. οἱ is ‘for him’. ἐπέκλωσεν is the aorist of ἐπικλώθω ‘spin to’, said of fate as a thread; τά γε ‘these things’. δαίμων is an unnamed divine power, neither a particular god nor a bare ‘fate’. The unit begins in the middle of line 64.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖ Θεσπρωτῶν ἀνδρῶν ἐκ νηὸς ἀποδρὰς
ἤλυθ’ ἐμὸν πρὸς σταθμόν, ἐγὼ δέ τοι ἐγγυαλίξω·
sentences.tr:
nyn au Thesprōtōn andrōn ek nēos apodras
ēlyth’ emon pros stathmon, egō de toi engyalixō·
sentences.l:
Now again, from a ship of Thesprotian men having run away,
he has come to my steading, and I to you will deliver him;
sentences.i: Now he has run away from a ship of Thesprotians and has come to my steading, and I will put him into your hands;
sentences.n: νῦν αὖ ‘now again’. Θεσπρωτῶν ἀνδρῶν ‘Thesprotian men’ are a people of the mainland. ἀποδράς is the aorist participle of ἀποδιδράσκω ‘run away’. ἤλυθ’ is ἤλυθε, an epic form of ἦλθε ‘came’. ἐμὸν πρὸς σταθμόν ‘to my steading’. ἐγγυαλίξω is a future of ἐγγυαλίζω ‘put into the hand’: Eumaeus hands the stranger over to Telemachus. The unit ends at the high stop at the end of line 66.

sentences.t: ἔρξον ὅπως ἐθέλεις·
sentences.tr: erxon hopōs etheleis·
sentences.l: do as you wish;
sentences.i: do as you wish;
sentences.n: Eumaeus leaves the decision to Telemachus. ἔρξον is the aorist imperative of ἔρδω ‘do’, and ὅπως ἐθέλεις is ‘as you wish’. The unit is half a line, closed by the high stop, and the speech moves at once to the stranger’s standing.

sentences.t: ἱκέτης δέ τοι εὔχεται εἶναι.
sentences.tr: hiketēs de toi euchetai einai.
sentences.l: and your suppliant he declares himself to be.”
sentences.i: and he declares himself your suppliant.”
sentences.n: ἱκέτης ‘suppliant’ is one who comes asking protection, which a host is bound to give. τοι is σοι, ‘to you’, that is ‘your’. εὔχεται εἶναι ‘declares himself to be’: εὔχομαι with the infinitive states a claim. With this word Eumaeus hands the stranger’s fate to Telemachus. The unit closes his speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The formula of line 30 returns: τὸν δ’ αὖ ‘to him in turn’, ἀντίον ‘face to face’, with πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ translated every time. Murray begins a new paragraph. The same line is found elsewhere in the poem with the same English.

sentences.t: Εὔμαι’, ἦ μάλα τοῦτο ἔπος θυμαλγὲς ἔειπες·
sentences.tr: Eumai’, ē mala touto epos thymalges eeipes·
sentences.l: “Eumaeus, truly this word, heart-paining, you have spoken;
sentences.i: “Eumaeus, you have spoken a word that truly pains my heart;
sentences.n: Telemachus answers. Εὔμαι’ is the vocative Εὔμαιε, elided. ἦ μάλα ‘truly’, as at line 8. θυμαλγές ‘heart-paining’ is built on θυμός and ἄλγος and agrees with ἔπος ‘word’. ἔειπες is an aorist of εἶπον, with the old double ε-. What pains him is the stranger’s request to be received, which he can hardly grant.

sentences.t: πῶς γὰρ δὴ τὸν ξεῖνον ἐγὼν ὑποδέξομαι οἴκῳ;
sentences.tr: pōs gar dē ton xeinon egōn hypodexomai oikōi;
sentences.l: for how indeed the stranger shall I receive in my house?
sentences.i: For how am I to receive the stranger in my house?
sentences.n: πῶς γὰρ δή ‘for how then’. ὑποδέξομαι is the future of ὑποδέχομαι ‘receive as a guest’, here a deliberative question. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. τὸν ξεῖνον: the article-form is a pronoun, ‘this stranger’. οἴκῳ is a dative, ‘in my house’. The unit ends at the question mark.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς μὲν νέος εἰμὶ καὶ οὔ πω χερσὶ πέποιθα
ἄνδρ’ ἀπαμύνασθαι, ὅτε τις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ·
sentences.tr:
autos men neos eimi kai ou pō chersi pepoitha
andr’ apamynasthai, hote tis proteros chalepēnēi·
sentences.l:
I myself am young, and not yet in my hands do I trust
to ward off a man, when anyone first grows angry;
sentences.i: I am young myself, and do not yet trust my hands to ward off a man, whenever someone is the first to grow angry;
sentences.n: αὐτὸς μέν ‘I myself, for my part’ is answered by μητρὶ δέ at line 73. πέποιθα is a perfect with present sense, ‘I trust’, taking the dative χερσί. ἀπαμύνασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἀπαμύνω ‘ward off’ and takes ἄνδρα. ὅτε τις … χαλεπήνῃ is a general clause with a subjunctive and no ἄν: ‘whenever anyone grows angry’. πρότερος ‘first’ is predicative. The unit ends at the high stop.

sentences.t:
μητρὶ δ’ ἐμῇ δίχα θυμὸς ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μερμηρίζει,
ἢ αὐτοῦ παρ’ ἐμοί τε μένῃ καὶ δῶμα κομίζῃ,
εὐνήν τ’ αἰδομένη πόσιος δήμοιό τε φῆμιν,
sentences.tr:
mētri d’ emēi dicha thymos eni phresi mermērizei,
ē autou par’ emoi te menēi kai dōma komizēi,
eunēn t’ aidomenē posios dēmoio te phēmin,
sentences.l:
and for my mother in two ways the heart in her mind is pondering,
whether right here beside me she should remain and keep the house,
respecting her husband’s bed and the people’s talk,
sentences.i: and my mother’s heart within her is divided in two, wondering whether to stay right here with me and keep the house, respecting her husband’s bed and the talk of the people,
sentences.n: The dative μητρὶ ἐμῇ ‘for my mother’ goes with θυμός ‘heart’. δίχα is ‘in two ways’; μερμηρίζει is ‘ponders, is in doubt’. The doubt is put as two alternatives, ἢ … ἦ (line 76); μένῃ and κομίζῃ are subjunctives. αὐτοῦ ‘right there’. αἰδομένη, a participle of αἰδέομαι, takes the accusatives εὐνήν ‘bed’ and φῆμιν ‘talk’. δήμοιο is a genitive in -οιο; δῆμος is the community, the people of the land. The sentence is cut at this comma because it would otherwise run to five lines.

sentences.t:
ἦ ἤδη ἅμ’ ἕπηται Ἀχαιῶν ὅς τις ἄριστος
μνᾶται ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἀνὴρ καὶ πλεῖστα πόρῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
ē ēdē ham’ hepētai Achaiōn hos tis aristos
mnatai eni megaroisin anēr kai pleista porēisin.
sentences.l:
or now to go along with whichever of the Achaeans is best,
a man who woos in the halls and gives most.
sentences.i: or whether she should go with him now, whichever of the Achaeans is the best man and woos her in the halls and gives the most gifts.
sentences.n: ἦ with the circumflex here means ‘or’, the second alternative, and not the ἦ ‘truly’ of line 69. ἤδη is ‘already, now’. ἕπηται is a subjunctive of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, here as a wife. ὅς τις ἄριστος ‘whoever is best’. μνᾶται is the third singular of μνάομαι ‘woo’, the verb behind μνηστῆρες ‘suitors’. πόρῃσιν is an aorist subjunctive of πορεῖν ‘give’; the thing given is understood, bridal gifts. The unit begins at line 76.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοὶ τὸν ξεῖνον, ἐπεὶ τεὸν ἵκετο δῶμα,
ἕσσω μιν χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε, εἵματα καλά,
δώσω δὲ ξίφος ἄμφηκες καὶ ποσσὶ πέδιλα,
πέμψω δ’ ὅππη μιν κραδίη θυμός τε κελεύει.
sentences.tr:
all’ ē toi ton xeinon, epei teon hiketo dōma,
hessō min chlainan te chitōna te, heimata kala,
dōsō de xiphos amphēkes kai possi pedila,
pempsō d’ hoppē min kradiē thymos te keleuei.
sentences.l:
But truly, the stranger, since your house he has come to,
I will clothe him in a cloak and a tunic, fine clothes,
and I will give a double-edged sword and sandals for his feet,
and I will send him where heart and spirit bid him.
sentences.i: But as for the stranger, since he has come to your house, I will clothe him in a cloak and a tunic, fine clothes, and give him a double-edged sword and sandals for his feet, and send him wherever his heart and spirit bid him.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι ‘but truly’ turns from the doubts to what he will do. τὸν ξεῖνον is the topic, ‘as for the stranger’. τεὸν is the epic possessive ‘your’ (Attic σόν). ἕσσω is a future of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, with μιν and then the clothes. ξίφος ἄμφηκες is a ‘double-edged’ sword, the second element being ἀκή ‘edge’. ποσσί is the dative plural of πούς in -σσι, πέδιλα are ‘sandals’. ὅππῃ ‘to whatever place’; κραδίη θυμός τε ‘heart and spirit’ take a singular verb.

sentences.t: εἰ δ’ ἐθέλεις, σὺ κόμισσον ἐνὶ σταθμοῖσιν ἐρύξας·
sentences.tr: ei d’ etheleis, sy komisson eni stathmoisin eryxas·
sentences.l: but if you wish, you take care of him, in the steadings having kept him;
sentences.i: but if you like, keep him in the steading and take care of him;
sentences.n: Telemachus offers Eumaeus the alternative. εἰ δ’ ἐθέλεις ‘but if you wish’. κόμισσον is an aorist imperative of κομίζω ‘take care of’, and ἐρύξας the aorist participle of ἐρύκω ‘keep, hold’. σταθμοῖσιν is a plural for the single steading. The unit ends at the high stop.

sentences.t:
εἵματα δ’ ἐνθάδ’ ἐγὼ πέμψω καὶ σῖτον ἅπαντα
ἔδμεναι, ὡς ἂν μή σε κατατρύχῃ καὶ ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr:
heimata d’ enthad’ egō pempsō kai siton hapanta
edmenai, hōs an mē se katatrychēi kai hetairous.
sentences.l:
and clothes here I will send, and food, all of it,
to eat, so that he not wear you down, and your companions.
sentences.i: and I will send clothes here, and all the food to eat, so that he may not wear you and your companions out.
sentences.n: εἵματα ‘clothes’ is the object of πέμψω ‘I will send’. σῖτον ἅπαντα is ‘all the food’, with ἔδμεναι, the epic infinitive of ἔδω ‘eat’, of purpose. ὡς ἂν μή with the subjunctive κατατρύχῃ means ‘so that he may not wear down’, and the objects are σε καὶ ἑταίρους, ‘you and your companions’, the other herdsmen. The sentence ends at the full stop.

sentences.t:
κεῖσε δ’ ἂν οὔ μιν ἐγώ γε μετὰ μνηστῆρας ἐῷμι
ἔρχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
keise d’ an ou min egō ge meta mnēstēras eōimi
erchesthai·
sentences.l:
But thither, among the suitors, I would not allow him
to go;
sentences.i: but I would not let him go there, among the suitors;
sentences.n: κεῖσε ‘thither’ has the suffix -σε of direction, and points to the town. ἂν … ἐῷμι is an optative of ἐάω ‘allow’, ‘I should not allow’. μετά with the accusative μνηστῆρας means ‘among’. The infinitive ἔρχεσθαι stands at the head of line 86, and the unit ends there at the high stop.

sentences.t: λίην γὰρ ἀτάσθαλον ὕβριν ἔχουσι·
sentences.tr: liēn gar atasthalon hybrin echousi·
sentences.l: for exceedingly wanton insolence they have;
sentences.i: for they have an exceedingly wanton insolence;
sentences.n: λίην is ‘exceedingly’. ἀτάσθαλον ‘wanton’ is the adjective behind ἀτασθαλίαι at the start of the poem. ὕβρις is ‘insolence’, a violent contempt for others. ἔχουσι ‘they have’. The unit gives the reason for keeping the stranger away. It begins in the middle of line 86.

sentences.t: μή μιν κερτομέωσιν, ἐμοὶ δ’ ἄχος ἔσσεται αἰνόν.
sentences.tr: mē min kertomeōsin, emoi d’ achos essetai ainon.
sentences.l: lest they taunt him, and for me grief will be fearsome.
sentences.i: for fear they may taunt him; that would be a fearsome grief to me.
sentences.n: μή with the subjunctive κερτομέωσιν is a clause of fear: ‘lest they taunt him’. The verb of fearing is not stated, and i supplies it. κερτομέω is ‘taunt’, uncontracted. ἐμοὶ δ’ ἄχος ἔσσεται αἰνόν ‘and grief will be fearsome for me’: ἄχος ‘grief’, αἰνός ‘fearsome’, ἔσσεται the future of εἰμί with a doubled σ.

sentences.t:
πρῆξαι δ’ ἀργαλέον τι μετὰ πλεόνεσσιν ἐόντα
ἄνδρα καὶ ἴφθιμον, ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτεροί εἰσι.
sentences.tr:
prēxai d’ argaleon ti meta pleonessin eonta
andra kai iphthimon, epei ē poly pherteroi eisi.
sentences.l:
And grievous it is to accomplish anything, among more men being,
a man, even a mighty one, since truly they are by far better.”
sentences.i: And it is grievous for even a mighty man to accomplish anything when he is among a greater number, since they are far superior.”
sentences.n: πρῆξαι is the aorist infinitive of πράσσω ‘accomplish’; its subject is ἄνδρα ‘a man’, and ἀργαλέον ‘grievous’ is the predicate. μετὰ πλεόνεσσιν ἐόντα ‘being among more’: πλεόνεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι. ἴφθιμον ‘mighty’. ἐπεὶ ἦ ‘since truly’; φέρτεροι is a comparative of ἀγαθός, ‘better, superior’. The unit closes Telemachus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe polytlas dios Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The reply-formula: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε ‘him then in turn addressed’. πολύτλας ‘much-enduring’ and δῖος ‘heavenly’ are Odysseus’ standing epithets and are translated each time. He is still disguised, and Telemachus does not know that the man he hears is his father. The same line is found elsewhere in the poem with the same English.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλ’, ἐπεί θήν μοι καὶ ἀμείψασθαι θέμις ἐστίν,
ἦ μάλα μευ καταδάπτετ’ ἀκούοντος φίλον ἦτορ,
οἷά φατε μνηστῆρας ἀτάσθαλα μηχανάασθαι
ἐν μεγάροις, ἀέκητι σέθεν τοιούτου ἐόντος.
sentences.tr:
ō phil’, epei thēn moi kai ameipsasthai themis estin,
ē mala meu katadaptet’ akouontos philon ētor,
hoia phate mnēstēras atasthala mēchanaasthai
en megarois, aekēti sethen toioutou eontos.
sentences.l:
“O friend, since, I suppose, for me also to answer it is the custom,
truly you rend, as I listen, my dear heart,
such wanton things as you say the suitors devise
in the halls, against your will, you being such a one.
sentences.i: “My friend, since it is the custom, I suppose, for me too to give an answer, you truly tear at my heart as I listen, with the wanton deeds you say the suitors are plotting in the halls against the will of one who is as you are.
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks in disguise. ὦ φίλ’ is ὦ φίλε with its final vowel elided, ‘O friend’. θήν is a particle ‘I suppose’; θέμις ἐστίν ‘it is the custom’, with the infinitive ἀμείψασθαι ‘to answer’. καταδάπτετ’ and φατε are second-person plural, though φίλ’ and σέθεν are singular; the Greek does not say whether Eumaeus is meant too. μευ ἀκούοντος is a genitive ‘as I listen’. ἀέκητι σέθεν ‘against your will’ takes a genitive, and τοιούτου ἐόντος ‘you being such a man’ agrees with σέθεν.

sentences.t:
εἰπέ μοι ἠὲ ἑκὼν ὑποδάμνασαι, ἦ σέ γε λαοὶ
ἐχθαίρουσ’ ἀνὰ δῆμον, ἐπισπόμενοι θεοῦ ὀμφῇ,
ἦ τι κασιγνήτοις ἐπιμέμφεαι, οἷσί περ ἀνὴρ
μαρναμένοισι πέποιθε, καὶ εἰ μέγα νεῖκος ὄρηται.
sentences.tr:
eipe moi ēe hekōn hypodamnasai, ē se ge laoi
echthairous’ ana dēmon, epispomenoi theou omphēi,
ē ti kasignētois epimempheai, hoisi per anēr
marnamenoisi pepoithe, kai ei mega neikos orētai.
sentences.l:
Tell me whether willingly you submit, or whether you, at least, the people
hate throughout the land, following a god’s voice,
or whether in any way you blame your brothers, in whom a man
trusts when they fight, even if a great quarrel arises.
sentences.i: Tell me whether you submit to this willingly, or whether the people hate you throughout the land, following some god’s voice, or whether you find some fault with your brothers, on whom a man relies when they are fighting, even if a great quarrel has arisen.
sentences.n: Three alternatives in one question, joined by ἠέ, ἦ and ἦ. ἑκών ‘willingly’. ὑποδάμνασαι is the second singular middle of ὑποδάμνημι ‘subdue’, ‘you submit’. ἐπισπόμενοι is an aorist participle of ἐφέπομαι ‘follow’; θεοῦ ὀμφῇ is ‘a god’s voice’, a divine utterance. ἐπιμέμφεαι is uncontracted, ‘you blame’; οἷσι is a relative, ‘in whom’; πέποιθε ‘trusts’; ὄρηται is an aorist subjunctive of ὄρνυμι ‘arise’. The first two alternatives are found elsewhere in the poem with the same English.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ ἐγὼν οὕτω νέος εἴην τῷδ’ ἐπὶ θυμῷ,
ἢ παῖς ἐξ Ὀδυσῆος ἀμύμονος ἠὲ καὶ αὐτός·
sentences.tr:
ai gar egōn houtō neos eiēn tōid’ epi thymōi,
ē pais ex Odysēos amymonos ēe kai autos·
sentences.l:
Would that I were so young, with this heart of mine,
either a child of blameless Odysseus, or even he himself;
sentences.i: If only I were so young, with this heart of mine, either the child of blameless Odysseus or Odysseus himself;
sentences.n: A wish, αἲ γάρ with the optative εἴην ‘would that I were’. οὕτω νέος is ‘so young’, ἐπὶ θυμῷ ‘with this heart’. The disguised Odysseus wishes to be either Odysseus’ child or Odysseus himself, and the poet lets him speak of himself in the third person. ἀμύμονος ‘blameless’ is a standing epithet whose true meaning is not known. Ὀδυσῆος has a single σ. Murray prints no line 101; the numbering runs from 100 to 102, and the text here follows him.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀπ’ ἐμεῖο κάρη τάμοι ἀλλότριος φώς,
εἰ μὴ ἐγὼ κείνοισι κακὸν πάντεσσι γενοίμην,
ἐλθὼν ἐς μέγαρον Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.tr:
autik’ epeit’ ap’ emeio karē tamoi allotrios phōs,
ei mē egō keinoisi kakon pantessi genoimēn,
elthōn es megaron Laertiadeō Odysēos.
sentences.i: then let a foreign man cut my head from me at once, if I did not prove a bane to every one of them by going to the hall of Odysseus, son of Laertes.
sentences.n: This completes the wish, and the line numbering skips 101, as Murray prints it. αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα ‘at once then’. τάμοι is an aorist optative of τάμνω ‘cut’, in a wish. ἀλλότριος φώς is ‘a foreign man’. εἰ μὴ … γενοίμην is ‘if I were not to become’; κείνοισι is the Ionic dative ‘to those’. Λαερτιάδεω is a patronymic in -εω: ‘the son of Laertes’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ αὖ με πληθυῖ δαμασαίατο μοῦνον ἐόντα,
βουλοίμην κ’ ἐν ἐμοῖσι κατακτάμενος μεγάροισι
τεθνάμεν ἢ τάδε γ’ αἰὲν ἀεικέα ἔργ’ ὁράασθαι,
sentences.tr:
ei d’ au me plēthui damasaiato mounon eonta,
bouloimēn k’ en emoisi kataktamenos megaroisi
tethnamen ē tade g’ aien aeikea erg’ horaasthai,
sentences.l:
But if in turn me by their numbers they overpowered, being alone,
I would prefer, having been killed in my own halls,
to be dead than these always unseemly deeds to look upon,
sentences.i: But if instead their numbers overpowered me, alone as I was, I would rather be killed in my own halls and be dead than keep seeing these unseemly deeds,
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ αὖ ‘but if, on the other hand’. δαμασαίατο is the third plural aorist optative middle of δαμάζω, with -αίατο for -αιντο. πληθυῖ is the dative of πληθύς ‘multitude’. μοῦνον ἐόντα ‘me being alone’. βουλοίμην κε ‘I would prefer’; κατακτάμενος is an aorist participle with passive sense, ‘killed’. ἐμοῖσι is ‘my own’. τεθνάμεν is the perfect infinitive ‘to be dead’ (Attic τεθνάναι); ὁράασθαι is the uncontracted infinitive of ὁράω; ἀεικέα ‘unseemly’. The unit ends at a comma because the sentence runs on to line 111 and would otherwise be seven lines long.

sentences.t:
ξείνους τε στυφελιζομένους δμῳάς τε γυναῖκας
ῥυστάζοντας ἀεικελίως κατὰ δώματα καλά,
sentences.tr:
xeinous te styphelizomenous dmōias te gynaikas
rhystazontas aeikeliōs kata dōmata kala,
sentences.l:
strangers roughly handled, and the maidservant women
(the men) dragging about in unseemly ways through the fine house,
sentences.i: strangers roughly handled, and the suitors dragging the maidservants about in unseemly ways through the fine house,
sentences.n: These accusatives continue the infinitive ὁράασθαι ‘to look upon’. ξείνους … στυφελιζομένους ‘strangers roughly handled’ is a passive participle. δμῳάς τε γυναῖκας are maidservants. ῥυστάζοντας ‘dragging about’ is masculine, so it cannot agree with the women; its subject, the suitors, is left to be understood, and l and i supply it. ἀεικελίως is ‘in unseemly ways’; κατὰ δώματα καλά ‘through the fine house’. The unit ends at a comma, and the sentence goes on.

sentences.t:
καὶ οἶνον διαφυσσόμενον, καὶ σῖτον ἔδοντας
μὰψ αὔτως, ἀτέλεστον, ἀνηνύστῳ ἐπὶ ἔργῳ.
sentences.tr:
kai oinon diaphyssomenon, kai siton edontas
maps autōs, ateleston, anēnystōi epi ergōi.
sentences.l:
and wine being drained, and (the men) eating food
without cause, just so, unaccomplished, over a never-finished work.”
sentences.i: and the wine being drained, and the men eating the food for no reason at all, with nothing achieved, in a business that is never finished.”
sentences.n: The accusatives go on: οἶνον διαφυσσόμενον ‘wine being drawn off’, and σῖτον ἔδοντας ‘eating food’, the participle again masculine with the suitors understood. μὰψ αὔτως: μάψ is ‘without cause’, αὔτως ‘just so’. ἀτέλεστον ‘unaccomplished’; ἀνηνύστῳ ‘never finished’, from ἀν- and ἀνύω. ἐπὶ ἔργῳ ‘over a work’ is compressed: the suitors consume without producing anything. The unit closes Odysseus’ speech.
